using-directive.md:22 "The `global` modifier has the same effect as adding the same `using` directive to every source file in your project."; project-sdk/overview.md:135 implicit global usings are added to new C# projects (ImplicitUsings=enable in DonHang.Api). Ledger text is right, but the lesson says a type from the file's own PROJECT needs no using: Program.cs (DonHang.Api project) has `using DonHang.Api;` and `using DonHang.Api.Middleware;`. JwtTokenService works in AuthController because DonHang.Api encloses DonHang.Api.Controllers.
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: The `using` lines are not a complete list: a type in the file's own namespace, or in a namespace that contains it, needs no `using`, and a project can add `using` lines for every file at once. So read the constructor's types too.

issues.text: Claim 6 overgeneralised in the prose. 'A type from the file's own project needs no using' is false: DonHang.Api/Program.cs, in the DonHang.Api project, needs `using DonHang.Api;` and `using DonHang.Api.Middleware;`. What holds is namespace lookup: `JwtTokenService` (namespace DonHang.Api) needs no using in AuthController because DonHang.Api encloses DonHang.Api.Controllers. Global/implicit usings (ImplicitUsings=enable) are a second gap the prose omits.
issues.quote: because a type from the file's own project needs no `using`, so read the constructor's types too
issues.fix: Replace the sentence with claim 6 suggested_text: "The `using` lines are not a complete list: a type in the file's own namespace, or in a namespace that contains it, needs no `using`, and a project can add `using` lines for every file at once. So read the constructor's types too." In Try it step 2, change "the controller's own project, `DonHang.Api`, needs no `using`" to "types from `DonHang.Api` itself need no `using` here, because the controller's namespace sits inside it".

issues.text: Definition contradicts section 5. 'Reaching' is any concrete object created with `new` in a field or a method, but OrderService.cs:12 does `var order = new Order { ... }` and lines 10/32 `throw new ArgumentException`/`KeyNotFoundException` inside methods, yet the lesson says OrderService 'passes all three checks'. Creating data objects and exceptions is not a dependency; the definition must be limited to collaborators the class calls.
issues.quote: creating a concrete object inside the class itself, for example with `new` in a field or a method, instead of asking for it
issues.fix: Core concepts: "reaching for a dependency — creating, inside the class itself, an object it calls to do its work (such as a notifier or a repository), for example with `new` in a field, instead of asking for it. Building data such as a new `Order` is not reaching." Mirror in claim 5 of meta.json.

issues.text: Option a overstates: `OrderService` does not receive everything it needs; it builds `new Order` itself (OrderService.cs:12). Key remains the best option, but a careful reader can object.
issues.quote: Everything it needs is passed in as a Domain interface
issues.fix: Option a en: "Every service it calls is passed in as a Domain interface"; vi: "Mọi service nó gọi đều được truyền vào dưới dạng interface của Domain".

issues.text: Claim 7 facts hold, but the sentence states as fact that Infrastructure's contract IS the interfaces it implements and that DonHangDbContext is its working detail. The repo declares no such boundary: DonHangDbContext is public, Program.cs:59 resolves it, ProductsController also takes it, and Infrastructure also offers `AddDonHangInfrastructure` to Program.cs.
issues.quote: In Đơn Hàng the infrastructure project's contract is the interfaces it implements from `DonHang.Domain`, such as `IOrderRepository`; `DonHangDbContext` is its own working detail.
issues.fix: "In Đơn Hàng, what the infrastructure project offers the rest of the code is mainly its implementations of interfaces from `DonHang.Domain`, such as `IOrderRepository`; `DonHangDbContext` is the class it uses to do that work." Mark the framing part of claim 7 kind opinion.

issues.text: Context says changing 'how that database class is set up' touches a dozen controllers, and option d's explanation repeats 'set up'. The controllers receive the class through their constructors, so changing its setup (its registration) would not touch them; what touches them is a change to the class's members they call. Key a is still the best answer.
issues.quote: Then the team needs to change how that database class is set up.
issues.fix: Context en: "Then the team needs to change what that database class exposes, for example renaming a table it offers." (vi to match); explanation d en: "...but it only changes what the same class exposes."

issues.text: Core concepts defines reaching as creating a concrete object inside the class with `new`, instead of asking for it. The third check then says 'Reaching into its details' for a class that takes another project's concrete class, and section 5 shows `AuthController` taking `DonHangDbContext` in its constructor, which by the definition is asking. Summary line 4 and q4 option a ('Classes reached into another project's concrete details', for controllers that take the class in constructors) use the same second sense. I cannot tell which meaning is right.
issues.quote: Reaching into its details ties them together more tightly with every such line
issues.fix: Keep 'reaching' only for creating with `new`. In the third check, summary line 4 and q4 option a (en+vi), say 'depending on its details' / 'depended on another project's concrete details' instead of 'reaching into'.

issues.text: The diagram has separate end nodes 'comment' and 'worth a question', and the first check draws that line carefully. But 'many' parameters goes to 'comment', while the prose says a long list 'is a reason to ask', and summary line 3 says 'worth asking about'. Likewise 'details' goes to 'comment', yet section 5 says for `AuthController` 'A reviewer can ask'. I cannot narrate the diagram and prose the same way.
issues.quote: A long list is a reason to ask what the class is responsible for, not a style complaint.
issues.fix: Point the 'many' arrow to the 'worth a question' node. For 'details', either point it to 'worth a question' too, or add one sentence to the third check saying it is worth a comment and change section 5's 'can ask' to match.

issues.text: The lesson points out `JwtTokenService` is a concrete class from the API project itself but never says what the checks conclude about it. By check 1 it looks like 'worth a question'; by check 3 it is not another project, so no issue. I had to work that out myself and was not sure.
issues.quote: It also takes `JwtTokenService`, a concrete class from the API project itself.
issues.fix: Add half a sentence after it: by the first check that is at most a question, and the third check does not apply because it is the controller's own project.

issues.text: Core concepts says a public contract is the types a project offers. Here the infrastructure project's contract is interfaces declared in `DonHang.Domain`, another project. I re-read this to see how Infrastructure can offer types it did not declare.
issues.quote: In Đơn Hàng the infrastructure project's contract is the interfaces it implements from `DonHang.Domain`, such as `IOrderRepository`
issues.fix: Add a few words: the interfaces are declared in Domain and Infrastructure offers implementations of them, so other projects use Infrastructure through them without naming its classes.

issues.text: The AuthController block has `using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc;` and `using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore;`, and the prose only discusses `using DonHang.Infrastructure;`. Since the third check is about bringing in other projects, I wondered whether these two lines are also 'details' I should flag.
issues.fix: Add one sentence after the block: the two `Microsoft.` lines bring in library namespaces, not Đơn Hàng projects; this lesson's third check looks at Đơn Hàng projects only.
